topic: Crocodile beat Luffy twice and nearly a third time, and each time Luffy only survived because someone else saved him
title: Luffy Never Beat Crocodile Alone
description: Chapters 179, 202 and 206 show Crocodile beating Luffy again and again, and each time a rescue turns the fight. The wiki's own count says Luffy only won because of luck and help.
comment: Did Luffy earn the win over Crocodile, or was it luck and help? Pick one.

lines.text: Luffy didn't beat Crocodile alone. He lost to him three times first.

shot.fallback: boy and a hooked warlord facing off

lines.text: Round one is chapter 179. Crocodile hits him with the hook.

shot.fallback: hooked man striking a boy in sand

lines.text: And Robin is the one who pulls him out of it.

shot.fallback: woman helping a boy off the sand

lines.text: Round two is chapter 202. Crocodile dries him out in the sun.

shot.fallback: boy collapsed in a dry desert

lines.text: The wiki says it was Luffy's own water pistol that brought him back.

shot.fallback: boy sipping water from a flask

lines.text: Round three is chapter 206. The hook is poisoned this time.

shot.fallback: warlord with a glowing green hook

lines.text: And again it's Robin who brings the antidote.

shot.fallback: woman handing over a small vial

lines.text: Three losses, three rescues, and not one of them was his own strength.

shot.fallback: three panels of a boy rescued

lines.text: People say that makes the win a fluke. But look at what he found.
The wiki says without his own trick against Logia sand, the third fight favors Crocodile too.
So the win is real, but it was built from help, and from Crocodile's pride.

shot.fallback: proud warlord looking down at a boy

lines.text: Which makes you wonder why a man that careful ever let this crew reach the capital.
Because Luffy didn't beat Crocodile alone. He lost to him three times first.

shot.fallback: boy and a hooked warlord facing off

self_check.hook: Contrarian claim: Luffy lost three times before winning
self_check.loop: last line restates the opening claim as a lead-in
